South Hero.metaDescription: Raccoons, bats, skunks, and squirrels in South Hero, VT — lake camps, orchard farms, and island homes on Lake Champlain. Same-day service — call us today.
South Hero.housing_era: The southern half of Grand Isle in Lake Champlain, with seasonal lake camps and cottages, year-round shore homes, orchard and dairy farmhouses inland, and a small village center on Route 2.
South Hero.geographic_features: Lake Champlain (the island is surrounded by the lake, with Keeler Bay on the east), Keeler Bay (broad bay and marina shore on the island's east side), Apple orchards and farmland (working farms across the island's interior), Island shoreline wetlands (marshy coves and points around the shore)

South Hero.wildlife_intro:
South Hero living is shoreline living, and raccoons know every camp and cottage on the island. They raid shore homes and trash, bats roost in camp and cottage attics all summer, and skunks and woodchucks work the orchards and gardens inland. Squirrels and mice are the winter problem in year-round homes, and camps closed from fall to spring regularly open to a season of animal signs.

Island seasons are sharp — proof a camp before you close it in fall, and check it early at spring opening before bats return to a familiar attic. Bat exclusion here is timed for spring or late August through November with one-way doors, full proofing happens in winter, and no colony work is done while pups cannot fly. Our crew makes island runs regularly in camp season, so call us to get on the schedule.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. faqs.q: When should South Hero camp owners have their place checked?
faqs.a: Twice a year is ideal — in fall before closing, to seal gaps and remove anything already inside, and at spring opening, before the summer colony and nesting season. Our crew does both checks for many island camps. A small gap found in October is a far cheaper fix than a bat colony in July.

North Hero.wildlife_intro:
North Hero is narrow enough that every home is near the water, and its wildlife is shoreline wildlife: raccoons working camps and shore homes, bats in cottage attics and the village's older houses, and skunks under porches across the island. Mice are the great winter problem in both camps and year-round homes, and woodchucks and muskrats appear along the banks and garden edges by City Bay and The Gut.

Camp rhythm rules here — close tight in fall, open carefully in spring, and time any bat work for spring or late August through fall with one-way doors, never during the flightless-pup weeks. Winter proofing is done on empty buildings, and our crew can handle it while you are away if you arrange access. If your island place sat quiet through an icy Lake Champlain winter, call us for an opening inspection.

faqs.q: Are mice really that serious in North Hero camps?

Grand Isle.wildlife_intro:
Grand Isle town sits between two shores, and raccoons, bats, and skunks make full use of both. Shore camps draw raccoons and summer bat colonies, the farm interior draws woodchucks, skunks, and barn raccoons, and year-round homes draw the fall rush of mice and squirrels. With water on both sides and woods in patches, animals are never far from any roof in town.

Our crew's advice here is seasonal and simple: proof camps and homes in the fall, check them at spring opening, and schedule bat exclusion for spring or late August through November — one-way doors, winter proofing, and no colony work while pups cannot fly. Shoreline wind and ice open new gaps most winters, so an annual look is worth it. Call us and we will put your place on the island run.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. faqs.q: What opens up gaps in Grand Isle homes over the winter?
faqs.a: Lake wind, ice, and freeze-thaw cycles lift flashing, crack old caulk, and shift camp foundations and skirting, creating exactly the small openings mice, bats, and squirrels need. Our crew re-checks those known weak points each spring and reseals them with durable, chew-proof materials built for shore weather.

Isle La Motte.wildlife_intro:
Isle La Motte is small, quiet, and mostly camps, so its wildlife work is camp work: raccoons in cottages and trash, bats returning to the same camp attics each summer, and mice and red squirrels occupying quiet buildings all winter. Skunks and woodchucks work the island's gardens and farm edges, and shoreline homes occasionally host muskrats along the bank. An unvisited camp here can go a full season with an animal problem nobody sees.

That is why fall proofing matters more on Isle La Motte than almost anywhere — seal it before you leave, and have our crew check it at opening. Bat exclusion is timed for spring or late August through fall with one-way doors, winter is for proofing empty camps, and no colony work happens while pups are flightless. Call us in late summer to get your camp on the closing list before the ferry-season rush ends.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Isle La Motte, VT?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. faqs.q: My Isle La Motte camp had bats last summer. When can they be removed?
faqs.a: Bats are removed by exclusion, not trapping — one-way doors let them leave at dusk and not return. That work is done in spring or from late August through fall, outside the weeks when young bats cannot yet fly. Winter is the time to finish sealing every gap. Our crew will inspect and tell you which window your camp falls in.

Alburgh.wildlife_intro:
Alburgh is nearly an island itself, wrapped in lake and marsh, and wildlife is dense on all sides. Raccoons and skunks are everyday calls in the village and on the farms, bats summer in camp and farmhouse attics, and beavers and muskrats work Mud Creek and the marshy shores. Woodchucks dig across the farm interior, and shore camps follow the familiar open-and-close pattern of animal surprises.

Fall proofing before the lake freezes and spring checks at camp opening are the two best investments here. Bat exclusion is timed for spring or late August through November with one-way doors, proofing is finished in winter, and no colony work is done while pups cannot fly. Beaver flooding on the creeks is best called in early, before spring water spreads. Our crew runs Alburgh with the islands, so call us for either shore.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Alburgh, VT?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. After an inspection, our crew can explain the options and the cost for your camp, cottage, or home in Alburgh, with no pressure to go ahead.

faqs.q: Do beavers cause flooding problems in Alburgh?
faqs.a: Yes, along Mud Creek and the smaller farm brooks, dams can back water into fields, yards, and camp roads, especially in spring. Our crew can assess whether a pond-leveling device will hold the water at a safe height or whether licensed trapping is needed — relocating furbearers is prohibited in Vermont, so we will not offer that.
